issues.explanation: Pain Recall implies the patient personally sustained bodily injury during the trauma, which is hard to reconcile with the trauma type being trauma to a loved one unless there was also direct physical injury to the patient. That is not otherwise supported by the profile.

Physical Vulnerability and permanent bodily damage imply the patient believes his own body was physically harmed. For a trauma-to-a-loved-one presentation, this is difficult to explain clinically without evidence that he was also directly injured.

Military Topics is a trigger that suggests a military/combat-linked trauma context, but no other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal item supports a military-related formulation. As a standalone item it feels disconnected from the rest of the profile.

Avoid Driving is plausible for motor-vehicle trauma, but here it lacks support from the trauma type and from the rest of the profile. With no transport-related trigger or memory content, it appears to target a symptom domain not otherwise represented.

For trauma to a loved one, visible injuries is a plausible trigger, but darkness and alcohol smell are not well anchored to the rest of the profile. Nothing in memory, threat, or appraisals suggests a dark-space or alcohol-related trauma context, so these triggers feel disconnected rather than part of a coherent loved-one trauma presentation.

Avoiding work/study is hard to reconcile with this patient's occupation as a paramedic unless the trauma is clearly tied to the workplace, but the rest of the profile frames the trauma as harm to a loved one rather than occupational trauma. Drug use is also insufficiently supported elsewhere in the profile: there are no other items indicating broad externalising coping or substance-related trigger context, making this strategy feel tacked on.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after trauma to a loved one, but this specific wording implies a direct causal role in the event. The rest of the profile does not provide supporting content suggesting he believes his own actions caused the loved one's trauma. The other appraisals are about damage and unreliability of self, so this item is the least integrated with the stated trauma type and surrounding node content.

Alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only trigger that suggests a substance-related context. The other trigger and memory items center on victims/injuries, which fits a paramedic exposed to injured loved ones or victims. Without any corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal content linked to alcohol, this item stands out as weakly connected to the rest of the trauma representation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Drug Use: take drugs
issues.explanation: Drug use can occur in PTSD, but here it is the only maladaptive strategy that implies substance misuse. The rest of the profile emphasizes work avoidance, suppression, sensory reliving, and hypervigilant threat responses. With no parallel alcohol/substance-related trigger, appraisal, or memory content, this item looks clinically disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, self-blame is plausible only if the patient had a clear perceived role in failing to protect or respond. In this profile, the other items describe reliving of victims/injuries, hypervigilance, and damaged-self beliefs, but nothing else indicates a responsibility-based trauma narrative. This makes the specific self-blame item the least coherent appraisal relative to the rest of the selected content.

vignette:
For fifteen years, Omar had been the paramedic you wanted to see when your world fell apart. Calm, competent, and kind, he had a steady hand and a reassuring presence that could bring order to the most chaotic scenes. That all changed seven months ago, on a rain-slicked Tuesday afternoon when the dispatcher called out an MVC on the interstate. He didn't know until he was kneeling on the wet asphalt, the smell of gasoline and antiseptic wipes filling his nostrils, that the teenager trapped in the driver's seat was his own son, Amir. He worked on him with a desperate, automatic focus, the sights and sounds of the extrication blurring into a nightmare. There are parts of that hour he simply cannot remember, blank spaces where the terror was too immense to form a coherent memory. What he does recall returns not as a thought but as a full-body experience: the specific angle of Amir’s broken arm, the cold feel of the rain, the scent of blood mixing with the sterile smell of the ambulance. Because these fragments returned with such sensory intensity, he began to see echoes of them everywhere; the smell from a first-aid kit or the sight of rain on a car windscreen could now bring the entire memory rushing back.

When Omar first returned to work, he believed he could push through it. Then, on a routine call for a construction worker who had fallen, the sight of the man’s compound fracture sent him reeling. In an instant, he was back on the interstate, the memory of his son’s injuries flooding him with such sensory reality that he could feel the phantom weight of the C-collar in his hands. The terror was identical, a cold wave that left him breathless and shaking. Each time an image from that day broke through with such force, it served as visceral proof for the thought that followed: a competent paramedic, a good father, would not be falling apart like this. It felt like a confirmation of his own profound failure. This sudden, vivid recall left him feeling intensely vulnerable, and for the rest of his shift, he was on high alert, his concentration shattered. He found himself constantly scanning his surroundings, choosing a seat in the breakroom that kept his back to a wall, a profound sense of threat having taken root where his confidence used to be. Feeling so profoundly unsafe, even in the familiar setting of his own station, was the most convincing proof he had that something inside him had broken beyond repair. This persistent feeling of danger also seemed to keep his mind primed for the worst, and on days when his vigilance was highest, the memories of the accident were hardest to keep at bay, as if his brain was rehearsing the trauma to prepare for the next one.

This feeling of being unsafe began to bleed into every corner of his life. He had come to believe that he had failed in his most fundamental duty, not just as a paramedic but as a father. The thought, *I should have protected him*, became a constant, corrosive presence in his mind. This conviction that he had failed made the world feel treacherous, and he started interpreting every unexpected event as a potential catastrophe. His wife placing a hand on his shoulder as he stared out the window would cause him to jolt with alarm, a reaction that horrified them both. The sense of being permanently on guard made it impossible for the memories to stay buried; his hypervigilance seemed to actively seek out reminders of the accident, making it easier for the intrusive images to break through. This constant state of threat served only to reinforce his belief that he was broken, as he felt that a normal person, a capable person, would not be living with this level of fear. He became convinced he couldn't rely on himself, that his instincts were broken and he was permanently damaged by what had happened. This conviction that he was fundamentally compromised meant that things he would have once dismissed—a distant siren, a car backfiring—now snagged his attention, each one feeling like a potential sign of another disaster he would be helpless to prevent.

His entire life is now organized around managing these intrusions and the overwhelming feelings they bring. The belief that he is no longer reliable has made his paramedic's uniform feel like a costume he is unworthy to wear, and he has started calling in sick, unable to face the possibility of failing another patient. His avoidance of the hospital has ironically made it a more powerful trigger; now, even driving past the building or seeing a picture of an ambulance can feel like a direct confrontation with his perceived failure. The antiseptic smell of the hospital, or even seeing a news report about an accident, functions as a powerful trigger, bringing on a fresh wave of memories and a spike in his vigilance. It is on days when he encounters one of these reminders that he is most likely to call in sick, or to start a new, physically punishing project at home, a desperate attempt to outrun the internal chaos the trigger has unleashed. In response to this onslaught from both his own mind and the outside world, he tries desperately to keep his thoughts at bay. He throws himself into grueling tasks around the house—demolishing a bathroom, building a deck—working until his body aches too much for his mind to race.

However, these attempts at control have only tightened the trap. The more he tries to suppress the thoughts of the accident, the more forcefully they erupt as sensory-laden flashbacks, his mind refusing to let go of the details he most wants to forget. His avoidance of work serves as daily proof of his own negative appraisal: each missed shift confirms his fear that he can't rely on himself anymore. This exhaustion and the failure of his coping strategies have only heightened his sense of being under constant threat, making him even more susceptible to triggers. Last week, his wife cut her finger while cooking, and the sight of the blood on her skin sent a jolt of pure panic through him, the memory of his son’s more grievous wounds instantly present. Omar finally sought help after his wife found him sitting in their half-finished kitchen, staring blankly at the wall, unable to account for the last two hours. He is terrified that the calm, capable man he once was is gone for good, but a small part of him hopes that therapy might help him find a way to live with the ghosts of that rainy Tuesday, and to once again be the husband and father his family deserves.

The vignette does not describe how Omar's negative beliefs about himself or the world make him more susceptible to triggers.
The vignette does not explain how the intrusive trauma memory leads to or reinforces Omar's negative appraisals of himself.
The vignette does not state that experiencing the trauma memory makes Omar more sensitive or hyper-aware of external triggers.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not state that encountering triggers directly leads Omar to engage in maladaptive coping strategies.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not describe how Omar's negative beliefs about himself or the world make him more susceptible to triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not explain how the intrusive trauma memory leads to or reinforces Omar's negative appraisals of himself.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not state that experiencing the trauma memory makes Omar more sensitive or hyper-aware of external triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not describe how Omar's general sense of threat or hypervigilance causes the intrusive trauma memories to occur.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not explain that Omar's feeling of being under threat causes or strengthens his negative beliefs about himself.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not state that Omar's use of maladaptive strategies makes him more sensitive or reactive to triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
